Where things get harder is when the app grows a backend shape: queues, retries, scheduled jobs, heavier compute, private networking. Vercel still relies on third-party partners for queuing (like Upstash or Inngest…

articles.author: Varun S
articles.description:
Every cloud architect is familiar with the siren song of Amazon S3: "Infinite scale at cents per gigabyte." It’s the foundational logic of the modern data lake. But as many organizations move toward lakehouse architectures like Apache Hudi or Delta Lake, they are hitting a brutal financial wall that doesn't show up on a simple price-per-GB calculator.
I call it the S3 API Tax.
When your data platform ingests millions of small files—a common byproduct of real-time streaming and Hudi commits—you aren't just paying for storage. You are paying for the PUT, GET, and LIST requests. At scale, the cost of the requests can actually exceed the cost of the storage itself.
The 4MB Secret: Why Block Aggregation is the Cure
Moving from Cold Buckets to Hot/Warm/Cold Architectures
Hot (SSD): Your active Hudi commits and latency-sensitive metadata.


Warm (Capacity Pool): Data that is recently active but "cooling," accessible at millisecond latency without refactoring code.


Cold (Native S3): Historical archives and deep partitions for massive scans.



Beyond the Bill: The Strategic Advantage of FlexClone
The Architect’s Verdict
If your data strategy involves small-file proliferation or high-velocity commits, moving directly to S3 is an expensive mistake. You need an "Intelligent Buffer"—a system that understands the difference between a file and a block.
Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP provides the enterprise features (Snapshots, Clones, Replication) we've relied on for decades, but applies them to the scale of the cloud. It’s time to stop paying the API tax and start architecting for operational gravity.
articles.title: The S3 API Tax: Why Your "Cheap" Data Lakehouse is Costing You a Fortune

Many jobs are labeled remote. Very few mean remote-from-anywhere.
Here are practical checks that help you spot true remote roles faster and avoid common red flags:
1) Read the location line
“US Remote,” “Remote (EU),” “LATAM only,” or “Remote within X countries” usually mean location restrictions.
If time zones are listed, that can also imply location limits, even when the role is technically remote.
Look for explicit language like: These aren’t guarantees, but they’re stronger indicators.
“worldwide remote”
“global remote”
“work from anywhere”
“fully asynchronous”
“distributed team across multiple countries.”
2) Treat salary as a clue, not a promise
A range like $100k–$250k often signals a US-centered market (not always, but often).
3) Watch the application form

articles.author: Liudas
articles.description:
What happened to ambition in QA?
5-10 years ago, QA engineers were breaking systems, crafting strategies, writing frameworks from scratch, and figuring out how to test SSO, caching, race conditions, and much more.  
Now? Scroll through LinkedIn and all you see is:
AI writes test plan
Self-healing tests
Generate tests in plain English
🧙 This tool (yes, that one you hear about daily) will reshape everything! Reinvent test automation!



I use AI tools daily. They help. But many of these so-called problems were solved a decade ago. And this new wave of hype? But it's just wrapping old ideas in new packaging.  
QA deserves higher ambition. Not just easier test writing. As I said, is not a problem for a long time.
articles.title: What happened to ambition in QA?
